scope: One additional Phyllidia varicosa for the species guide, isolated inspection and optional identification. Its raised ridges, paired rhinophores, sheltered lateral gills and striped foot provide complementary top and underside details. No reef population or engine metadata is added.
iucnYearConvention: SeaLifeBase lists global Not Evaluated in IUCN Version 2025-2. No assessment date is supplied; iucnYear and iucnDateAssessed are null. This is not a Least Concern assessment or a statement that local populations face no threats.

specimens.name: Varicose phyllidia
marks: Blue-grey ridges with yellow-tipped knobs run lengthwise over a dark body
Two yellow, finely layered rhinophores stand near the front
The gills sit below the mantle edge, with no feathery plume on the back
A black stripe runs lengthwise along the underside of the foot
specimens.role: A small reef predator that feeds on sponges.
specimens.fact: The two yellow rhinophores sense chemicals in seawater. Its breathing gills sit under the mantle edge, away from the top of the back.
specimens.habitat: Tropical coral reefs across the Indo-West Pacific, including the Red Sea and central Pacific.
specimens.diet: Sponge tissue. Feeding on Axinyssa cf. aculeata has been observed on Indonesian coral reefs.
specimens.behavior: Glides on its broad foot and can draw its rhinophores into pockets. Feeding observations show the body contracting as it takes food from a sponge.
specimens.observe: Follow the raised central ridge, then compare the tucked-away gills with the feathery back gills of Anna’s chromodoris. In an underside view, look for the dark line along the foot.

claimSupport.acceptedName: Current WoRMS lists Phyllidia varicosa Lamarck, 1801 as the accepted target of several synonyms. OBIS independently links the accepted name to WoRMS 212835. The author is not parenthesised because the original genus is retained.
claimSupport.morphology: Brunckhorst’s museum revision and Rudman’s species account describe three to six longitudinal blue-grey ridges bearing yellow-capped tubercles, a black foot stripe and 27–30 lamellae on the rhinophoral clavus. The model is a representative variant; exact counts and colour intensity are not universal field rules.
claimSupport.variation: Papu et al. (2022) examined 114 specimens: their larger animals had more ridges, yellow concentrated on median tubercles, and a foot stripe sometimes broken into sections. Adults often curl the lateral mantle edge underneath. The illustrated continuous stripe and selected ridge layout are not claimed to be invariant.
claimSupport.gills: Rudman’s expert account places the secondary gills along the groove between mantle and foot. The posterior dorsal papilla is not a gill plume. The model must not inherit the exposed dorsal plume of the existing Chromodoris annae model.
claimSupport.sensory: California Academy of Sciences explains that the anterior rhinophores detect chemicals in water and that sea slugs move on a foot. This supports the general sensory and locomotion wording, not a species-specific detection threshold or movement rate.
claimSupport.feeding: Yasman (2003) directly observed this species feeding on Axinyssa cf. aculeata on Indonesian coral reefs, with body contraction and rhinophore withdrawal. The cf. qualification is retained; this observation does not mean every sponge is suitable prey.
claimSupport.rangeAndDepth: Rudman’s museum account gives the Indo-West Pacific including central Pacific and Red Sea. Its photographed specimens include 4–10 m and 22 m localities; an expert-confirmed South African record is at 25 m. The model-reference interval [4,25] represents those observations, not an exhaustive depth range or physiological limit. SeaLifeBase’s narrower cited 10–20 m interval is not treated as a limit.
claimSupport.size: The nominal .06 m is full posed body length, not height or foot width. It is close to the museum’s documented 58 mm individual. That account also records a 104 mm specimen, and Papu et al. document animals up to 87 mm in their collection. SeaLifeBase’s explicitly assumed 70 mm maximum is therefore not repeated as a species maximum.
claimSupport.conservation: The current SeaLifeBase summary gives global NE and no assessment date. No unaccessed IUCN rationale, trend, generic reproductive account, modelled fishing vulnerability or handling guidance is used.
claimSupport.comparison: The new one-way link to the existing Anna’s chromodoris entry compares raised ridges and sheltered gills with that animal’s smooth pattern and exposed plume. It is an educational comparison, not a claim that it is the closest relative or hardest real-world identification.

specimens.caution: Similar phyllidiids can require more than colour to distinguish. This is an illustrative adult-form specimen, not a taxonomic key. The fixed body/root and gentle appendage movement do not simulate locomotion, feeding, retraction or a universal current response. No sex, toxicity, handling, aquarium-care, medicinal, lifespan or reproductive claims are introduced.
